conclusion.detail: The loader that loaded a rewritten net.minecraft class is the same object as ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader(). appendToSystemClassLoaderSearch therefore targets the loader that actually resolves the game's classes, so ADG-1's second candidate rests on a premise that holds for the pinned launch. This measurement does not implement it and does not compare it against candidate 1 on any other ground.
conclusion.summary: In the pinned launch there is no parent/child split between an application loader and a system loader. There is one loader, and it is both.

correctsPriorAssertion.detail: jvm/README.md says stock Minecraft 26.1 runs on the application class loader 'which delegates to the system loader, so it finds that same copy'. The copy is found, so the consequence the sentence draws is right. The mechanism it names is not: delegation implies two loaders, and the launch has one object playing both parts. The correction matters because ADG-1's candidate 2 was read as blocked by that sentence, and it is not.
correctsPriorAssertion.measuredInstead: The two are the same object, so the resolution needs no delegation at all.

deviations.summary: The loader line is reported only when -Dravel.report.loader=true is set, so this launch carried three JVM arguments rather than the two ADG-5 describes. The extra one is a measurement switch that changes no rewrite and no launch argument the launcher builds; an ordinary launch without it prints exactly the line evidence/m2/prism-launch.json recorded.

The launcher rebuilds the instance's natives directory during launch preparation and puts its own -Djava.library.path after the instance's, which is the deviation evidence/m2/prism-launch.json already recorded. A library staged before launching is therefore gone by the time the JVM starts. This launch staged it from the wrapper command instead, which runs after that rebuild and immediately before the JVM. That is a capture aid: it adds no component and changes no launch argument.

The run was ended with SIGTERM at the title screen rather than by quitting the game, because the question is decided as soon as one target class is loaded and the JVM runs its shutdown hooks either way. No world was created, opened, or saved, so this record proves nothing about world lifecycle and does not restate what evidence/m2/prism-launch.json proved about it.

measurement.detail: Transformer.transform receives the loader that is defining the class it is asked to rewrite. It previously discarded that argument. It now records the loader's class and identity hash, the system loader's, whether the two are the same object, and the parent chain, at the moment of the first rewrite and as text rather than as a reference. The agent prints it from the shutdown hook that already reports what it rewrote.
measurement.method: in-process, from the class file transformer the JVM calls
measurement.takenOn: one launch of the pinned vanilla instance through the stock launcher

rewrite.detail: The counts are the agent's own, from the same shutdown report. They are here because a loader identity recorded by a launch that rewrote nothing would describe no rewrite, and the count is what rules that out.

summary: The loader that loaded a rewritten net.minecraft class in the official game process is the same object as ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader(), so the pinned launch has one loader where jvm/README.md describes a delegating pair.
whatThisDoesNotSay: Nothing here selects between ADG-1's two candidates. It removes an objection to the second one and says nothing about whether the first is preferable on any other ground.

Nothing here shows that appendToSystemClassLoaderSearch works. It shows that the loader that method targets is the loader that resolves the game's classes; whether an appended entry is then found by a class already loaded is a separate question this launch did not ask.
Nothing here is measured on a modded instance. A pack that installs another mod loader may introduce a loader this launch does not have, and the ATM11 instance was not launched.
The identity hashes are this process's. They differ on every run and prove only that two references are or are not the same object within one launch.

Nothing here says a rewritten class is loaded by this loader at every point in a session. The identity is the first rewrite's, which happened during startup; a class loaded later by a loader the game creates itself would not be visible in this record.
Nothing here measures the dedicated server. The launch was the client, and the loader arrangement of a server launch was not observed.
